title: Learning Mixture Models via Efficient High-dimensional Sparse Fourier Transforms
text: back to the landmark work of Pearson from 1894 on learning Gaussian mixture models [ pearson1894contributions ] in one dimension. Learning high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures was a central question in statistical learning, starting with the pioneering work of Dasgupta [ dasgupta1999learning ] . And starting with the same work, a significant effort has been focused on finding techniques that avoid “overfitting” to the assumption of Gaussianity on the cluster distributions. Mixture models have also served as a testing ground and often the first striking application for some of the most versatile tools developed for algorithms in statistical estimation. Classical examples include low-rank projections and spectral methods [ vempala2002spectral , kannan2005spectral , achlioptas2005spectral ] (that apply more generally to all log-concave distributions), random projections and the method of moments [ kalai2010efficiently , moitra2010settling , belkin2010polynomial ] (that are restricted to distributions with known moment relations), and tensor decompositions [ hsu2013learning ] (that need milder but still Gaussian-like low-order moments). In recent years, with a renewed focus on robust statistics [ diakonikolas2019robust , LaiRaoVempala ] , learning mixture models served as the central challenge [ DVWSimonsVignette ] . It led to the development of the method of spectral filtering [ diakonikolas2023algorithmic ] and the sum-of-squares method for robust statistics [ kothari_outlier-robust_2017 , kothari_better_2017 , hopkins2018mixture ] that eventually led to the full resolution of the question [ bakshi2020outlier , bakshi2022robustly ] via connections to algorithmic properties related to verifying concentration and anti-concentration [ karmalkar_list-decodable_2019 , raghavendra_list_2019 ] of high-dimensional probability distributions.
